notes: \cpara{Opens with the advice ``Persevere,'' which the author says high achievers give, and admits to not understanding it at first.}
\cpara{Reports that the author cannot work 14-hour days, and for years took this to mean a lack of perseverance.}

\cpara{Lists what the author's 1998 self said in reply, ending with a guess marked ``Perhaps'': that famous scientists praise hard work because it would be ``too awful'' if it counted for less than intelligence.}
\cpara{States the turn of the post as memoir: the author understood perseverance on finding that the important problems had been overestimated.}

\clogic{Stated without a hedge. The evidence the post gives is that the problems came to seem easier: they ``have seemed to become less intimidating,'' and ``The apparent difficulty of problems may go way down.'' The post reports no problem solved, and grants that ``you don't know how much work will be left when the confusion clears.'' That supports the claim that the problems came to look less difficult. ``Overestimated the difficulty'' claims more.}

\cpara{Lists the author's first picture of the task. The early writing bears out the timescale. ``Staring into the Singularity'' (first written in 1996; the archived text has later revisions) says: ``The generally accepted estimate has been and remains 2035 - less than forty years!'' It adds that ``many, including I, think that the Singularity may occur substantially sooner.''}

\cpara{Names the failure mode: meeting a problem one does not understand by imagining an enormous resource thrown at it, big enough to feel equal to the problem. The quadrillion-dollar example is an unnamed member of ``the AI list,'' given in the author's paraphrase.}
\cpara{Applies the failure mode to the author's own start.}

\cpara{The two figures agree (55 million divided by 365 is about 150,700). They are close to UN estimates for the late 1990s, about 52 million deaths a year (Our World in Data). On these figures an hour is about 6,250 deaths.}
\cpara{Repeats, nearly word for word, the first sentence of the paragraph before.}

\cpara{The dates check. The author announced ``Coding a Transhuman AI'' on the Extropians mailing list on 7 September 1998, as ``A fairly massive tome, about halfway complete at 210K,'' with the alternative title ``The Art of Seed AIs.'' Go2Net's purchase of Hypermart was reported in August 1998 (Telecompaper).}
\cfact{Nick Bostrom's \textsc{Superintelligence} (2014) agrees: ``This term was introduced by Eliezer Yudkowsky'' (as quoted in Wikipedia, ``Recursive self-improvement'').}

\cpara{``The Plan to Singularity'' (1999, revised 2000) matches this account: an open-source AI architecture, a line of programming languages called Flare, and a proposed Singularity Institute, which the document's later note says was created ``in July 2000.''}
\cpara{Judges the strategy in one line without saying why. The post's point does not depend on the reason.}
\cpara{Gives the change in outlook: from nothing to be done to a possible incremental path.}

\cpara{States the lesson in careful form: the ``apparent pathway'' shortened, and the problem ``looked'' less impossible. The record bears out the shortening. The 1996 essay gives 2035; the 1999 plan says ``we should plan to develop a seed AI by 2010.''}

\cpara{The second example, Friendly AI. It agrees with the book's earlier account in ``That Tiny Note of Discord,'' where the author of 1997 ``believed that any superintelligence would automatically do what was `right'\,''.}
\cpara{Sums up the change: Friendly AI went from ignored as impossible to taken on as extremely difficult.}

\cpara{The third example: understanding intelligence precisely, once written off as impossible, then taken on, as told in ``My Bayesian Enlightenment.'' The aside about ``AIfolk'' links to ``Above-Average AI Scientists,'' which the book does not include.}
\cpara{Reconciles two trends: single problems came to seem smaller while the whole task grew, as problems moved from the ``impossible'' list to the ``to do'' list.}

\cpara{Reports seeing other AI researchers call ``Impossible!'' problems that seemed to the author ``eminently solvable.'' No problem or researcher is named, and the link goes to the Star Wars parody of four days earlier, ``Use the Try Harder, Luke.'' The reader has the author's report and the author's judgment of the problems.}
\cpara{Introduces two senses of ``impossible.''}
\cpara{Places all the author's own uses in the second sense, ``I can't see any way to do that.'' The first sense covers impossibility proved from accepted laws, as the gears example below shows.}
\cpara{The central argument, stated with its conditions: the gain comes only ``if'' you avoid blind alleys and ``if'' you have the needed ability, and what falls is the ``apparent'' difficulty.}
\cpara{Asserts that the effect is strongest on confusing problems. The reason comes two paragraphs later.}

\cpara{Sets aside problems whose impossibility follows from understanding, such as a perpetual motion machine made of gears. The link goes to the author's post on the second law of thermodynamics, which makes that argument.}

\cpara{Gives the reason: a count of zero solutions measures confusion, and ``Confusion exists in the map, not in the territory.'' The paragraph grants that the remaining work is unknown. That is its case against the word ``impossible''; it does not promise that the work will be small.}
\cpara{Repeats the conditions and the conclusion of the paragraph beginning ``Any time you don't understand a domain,'' again with ``may'' and ``seem.''}
\cpara{Adds the step that closes the cycle: a problem that seems impossible is not tried, so the work that would change how it looks is not done.}
\cpara{Applies the cycle to the author: only a ``driven frame of mind'' kept the author at the problem long enough to become less intimidated.}
\cpara{Grants that the author also underestimated the whole task at the start, and calls the combination luck. It is the same distinction as before between single problems and the whole.}
\cpara{Contrasts the author with most AGI researchers, who are said not to be driven in this way.}

\clogic{A claim about why most people in a field are in it, offered with ``By and large'' and no evidence here. The linked post, ``Above-Average AI Scientists,'' gives the author's impressions of AGI conferences and concludes that ``AGI attracts people who fail to comprehend the difficulty of AGI.''}

\cpara{Credits Richard Hamming, with a link to his talk ``You and Your Research'' (1986). In the talk Hamming asked colleagues at lunch, over several weeks, ``What are the important problems of your field?'', then ``What important problems are you working on?'', and later why, if their work was not important, they were ``at Bell Labs working on it.'' The post's two questions are a fair summary.}
\cpara{Describes important problems: they look intimidating and promise neither publications nor progress.}

\cpara{Says the most important problems are often ``impossible,'' and gives one example: this, it says, is why more philosophers do not work on reductionist decompositions of consciousness. No evidence is offered for that explanation.}

\clogic{Hamming, whom the post has just cited, drew the line elsewhere: ``It's not the consequence that makes a problem important, it is that you have a reasonable attack.'' A problem with no visible attack, the post's second sense of ``impossible,'' is on Hamming's account not an important problem. The same difference is noted at ``Einstein's Superpowers.''}
\cpara{The first warning: talent only buys a seat, the stake is years of your life, and ``you can lose.''}
\cpara{Declines to recommend the impossible to everyone: most people, most of the time, should ``stick to the possible.''}
\cpara{Rejects ``Never give up'' and points back to ``Just Lose Hope Already'' (2007), which argues for knowing when to quit. The two posts agree.}
\cpara{States when there may be cause for the attempt: when something is worse than a wasted life, or is wanted more than ``thirty chips'' of years.}
\cpara{Adds that perseverance keeps things difficult, and warns readers not to ``needlessly plunge headlong'' into such a life.}
\cpara{Returns to the opening: perseverance has a part beyond working 14 hours a day.}
\cpara{Explains why the author missed this: what we notice about ourselves follows salience, not only self-image.}
\cpara{Gives what showed the author the other timescales: the researchers described earlier in the post.}
\cpara{Defines perseverance at the timescale of seconds and at the timescale of years.}
\cpara{Sets out three steps with their timescales: not running away (seconds), working (hours), sticking at it (years).}
\cpara{Ends with the author's record on the three steps. It agrees with the opening: the hours are the struggle, and the years come naturally.}
